notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Psalm 35, drawn from the sources retrieved.

---

## Overview / Structure

**Tripartite division.** Both Spurgeon and the Pulpit Commentary note that the psalm falls into three sections, each containing complaint, prayer, and a promise of praise: vv. 1–10, 11–18, and 19–28. Spurgeon likens the threefold repetition to Christ praying three times in Gethsemane with the same words. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-35.html)

**Authorship debate.** The traditional reading (Gill, Spurgeon, Guzik) holds that David wrote this while being hunted by Saul, pointing to the phrasing of v. 1 being nearly identical to 1 Samuel 24:15. Meanwhile, Ellicott states that "few good critics consider the psalm Davidic" and notes some ascribe it to Jeremiah or a later community facing foreign influence. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

**Imprecatory nature.** This is one of the so-called imprecatory psalms, calling down curses on enemies. Spurgeon robustly defends the language: "Viewing sinners as men, we love them and seek their good, but regarding them as enemies of God, we cannot think of them with anything but detestation … No loyal subject can wish well to rebels." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

**v. 1 — "Contend with my opponents, O LORD; fight against those who fight against me."**

The language is both legal and military. Gill notes that the Hebrew verb for "contend" (or "plead") is a legal term: David asks the Lord to take up his case in the courtroom as well as on the battlefield. He applies it to Christ, who "pleaded not his own cause as man, but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously," and to believers whose Advocate pleads against Satan the accuser. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

Ellicott points out that the verb for "fight" literally means "devour" (cf. Numbers 24:8: "He shall eat up the nations"), a vivid image of consuming enemies in battle. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

Guzik cites Maclaren, who notes that the prayer in v. 1a uses the same word and metaphor as David's remonstrance with Saul in 1 Samuel 24:15, and VanGemeren, who observes that "'contend' is a legal term, frequently used among the prophets." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Spurgeon: "Every saint of God shall have this privilege: the accuser of the brethren shall be met by the Advocate of the saints." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 2 — "Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid."**

The two defensive weapons (Hebrew *magen* = small shield, *tsinnah* = large body-covering shield) picture God interposing Himself between David and his enemies. Ellicott notes the poetic boldness of arming God with two shields at once — a "lapse" excused by the vividness of the imagery, "more vividly realised here than anywhere else except Isaiah 63:1." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

Gill says the point is not that God needs weapons, but that "he would be as these to David … their shield and buckler: he gives unto them the shield of salvation." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

Spurgeon: "The greater and lesser protections of providence may be here intended … This poetic imagery shows how the Psalmist realised the existence and power of God; and thought of him as a real and actual personage, truly working for his afflicted." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 3 — "Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers; say to my soul: 'I am your salvation.'"**

Now David calls for offensive weapons. Spurgeon pictures God blocking a defile with a lance so the weaker brother can escape: "What a glorious idea is this of Jehovah blocking the way of persecutors, holding them at the pike's end!" (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

Ellicott discusses the obscure Hebrew word *segor* (BSB "javelin"). He notes many modern scholars treat it as a noun equivalent to the Greek *sagaris* (a Persian/Scythian battle-axe or curved sword), making "an excellent parallelism" with "spear" — both offensive weapons. But the ancient versions (LXX, Vulgate) read it as "stop the way." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

The NET Bible notes confirm this uncertainty: the term occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28)

**"Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation.'"** This is the tender inner side of God's warlike activity. Maclaren (via Guzik): "This armed Jehovah, grasping shield and drawing spear, utters no battle shout, but whispers consolation to the trembling man crouching behind his shield." G. Campbell Morgan: "So trying were the circumstances … that he was at least in danger of losing his assurance in God. Hence the plea that God would give him the inward sense of certainty." Guzik lists six aspects of David's assurance: he had doubts, was not content with them, knew where to go for assurance, and knew assurance had a divine source and was deep and personal and present, not future. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Gill expands extensively: even believers who know Christ is the Saviour "sometimes … are at a loss about their interest in it … yet most earnestly desire the Lord would show it to them, and assure them of it; which favour, when granted, is by the witnessings of the Spirit to their spirits." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

---

**v. 4 — "May those who seek my life be disgraced and put to shame; may those who plan to harm me be driven back and confounded."**

The four verbs in this verse are understood by the NET Bible as jussives (prayer-wishes calling down judgment). Spurgeon insists "there is nothing malicious here, the slandered man simply craves for justice … Shameful disappointment shall be the portion of the enemies of the gospel." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php; https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28)

Gill treats these as prophecies of what would happen: Saul was indeed filled with shame when David held up the cut skirt of his robe (1 Samuel 24). He also applies it to Christ's enemies: the Jews who sought His life will be ashamed when they "see him come in the clouds of heaven, whom they have pierced." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

---

**v. 5 — "May they be like chaff in the wind, as the angel of the LORD drives them away."**

Chaff imagery recalls Psalm 1:4 — the worthless, weightless character of the wicked. Spurgeon: "Ungodly men are worthless in character, and light in their behaviour … it is but just that those who make themselves chaff should be treated as such." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

**"The angel of the LORD."** Here the traditions differ significantly:

- Guzik (Pentecostal/Evangelical), citing Boice, calls this "a preincarnate manifestation of the second person of the Trinity, the Lord Jesus Christ." Kidner (Anglican Evangelical) adds: "The angel of the Lord is either our salvation or our doom; cf. Exodus 23:20-22." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

- Gill gives three possibilities: a good angel executing God's orders, an evil angel "employed by the Lord as the executioner of his wrath," or simply a personification of divine judgment. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

- Ellicott takes a more naturalistic view: the "angel of Jehovah" is "a personification of the 'hurricane' itself, which drives before it all obstacles." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

- Spurgeon blends both: "Fallen angels shall haunt them, good angels shall afflict them." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 6 — "May their path be dark and slick, as the angel of the LORD pursues."**

The imagery is of a dangerous mountain pass in a storm. Ellicott notes that "the tracks in the limestone hills of Palestine are often worn as smooth as marble" (quoting Kay). Spurgeon: "What terrors are gathered here! No light, no foothold, and a fierce avenger at their heels!" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 7 — "For without cause they laid their net for me; without reason they dug a pit for my soul."**

The twice-repeated "without cause" is the nerve of David's pain. Kidner: "'Without cause,' twice here, and again in 19, touches the very nerve of David's pain … The psalms make us specially sensitive to the hurt of injustice." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Both Ellicott and the NET Bible note a textual issue: the Hebrew literally reads "they hid for me the pit of their net," which is awkward. Ellicott (and NET) suggest transposing "pit" and "net" between the two clauses for better sense and rhythm: "For unprovoked they hid a net for me, / Unprovoked they digged a pit for my soul." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm; https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28)

Spurgeon laments the effort the wicked put into their schemes: "Net-making and pit-digging require time and labour, and both of these the wicked will expend cheerfully if they may but overthrow the people of God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 8 — "May ruin befall them by surprise; may the net they hid ensnare them; may they fall into the hazard they created."**

This is the *lex talionis* — the trap snapping on the trapper. Gill: "So Haman was hanged on the same gallows he had prepared for Mordecai." The Hebrew word for "ruin" (*shoah*) primarily means a sudden storm or crash. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

Guzik applies this to spiritual warfare: "We may rightly pray that the devil is caught in and by his own snares and strategies (1 Timothy 3:7, 2 Timothy 2:26, 2 Corinthians 2:11)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Spurgeon: "How often Satan outwits himself, and burns his fingers with his own coals! This will doubtless be one of the aggravations of hell, that men will torment themselves with what were once the fond devices of their rebellious minds." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 9 — "Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation."**

Spurgeon is careful: "We do not triumph in the destruction of others, but in the salvation given to us of God. Prayer heard should always suggest praise." Gill sees this rejoicing specifically in "his salvation" — the finished work of Christ in which "the law is fulfilled, justice is satisfied, sin is atoned for … an everlasting righteousness is brought in." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

---

**v. 10 — "All my bones will exclaim, 'Who is like You, O LORD…'"**

Total-body praise. Spurgeon: "As if the tongue were not enough to bless God with, David makes every limb vocal … Those bones which were to have been broken by my enemies shall now praise God." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

Ellicott: "'All my bones' — as we say, 'all the fibres of my body.'" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

Gill sees the "poor and needy" as spiritually poor — those delivered from sin (too strong for them), from Satan (the strong man armed), and from every oppressor. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

---

**v. 11 — "Hostile witnesses come forward; they make charges I know nothing about."**

"False witnesses" is the ancient weapon against God's people. Gill: "To please Saul, there were always men to be found mean enough to impeach David." He also applies this to Christ before the Sanhedrin (Matthew 26:59) and to the apostles (Acts 24:5). Spurgeon: "He had not even a thought of sedition; he was loyal even to excess; yet they accused him of conspiring against the Lord's anointed." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 12 — "They repay me evil for good, to the bereavement of my soul."**

Gill notes the literal sense of "bereavement" (or "spoiling"): making his soul fatherless, i.e., comfortless (cf. John 14:18). Guzik, citing Horne, sees Christ foreshadowed: "This was never more literally true of David, than it was of the holy Jesus, when, standing before Pontius Pilate, he received no other return from the Jews … than that of being slandered, and put to death." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

---

**v. 13 — "Yet when they were ill, I put on sackcloth; I humbled myself with fasting, but my prayers returned unanswered."**

The last clause ("my prayers returned unanswered" in BSB; KJV: "my prayer returned into mine own bosom") has been interpreted several ways:

- Gill: Either (a) David prayed privately and heartily and his prayer was heard and answered, or (b) his prayer was slighted by his enemies and "returned back to himself, as a present despised is returned." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

- Ellicott rejects the idea of fruitless prayer. He prefers the meaning "my prayer came back again and again to my bosom" — i.e., it was repeated over and over. He also notes the literal interpretation of Ewald and Delitzsch: the prayer was muttered into his bosom, referring to a posture of bowed mourning. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

- Spurgeon: "Prayer is never lost: if it bless not those for whom intercession is made, it shall bless the intercessors. Clouds do not always descend in showers upon the same spot from which the vapours ascended … If our dove find no rest for the sole of her foot among our enemies, it shall fly into our bosoms and bring an olive branch of peace." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

The NET Bible renders it "but my prayer was returning upon my chest," noting the imperfect verb sets this line apart from the surrounding perfect-tense verbs describing past actions. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28)

---

**v. 14 — "I paced about as for my friend or brother; I was bowed down with grief, like one mourning for his mother."**

David's sympathy for his enemies was deep and genuine. Guzik suggests this may refer to David playing the harp to soothe Saul's troubled spirit. Spurgeon: "How few professors in these days have such bowels of compassion; and yet under the gospel there should be far more tender love than under the law." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 15 — "But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee…"**

The BSB "assailants I did not know" masks a notorious textual difficulty. The Hebrew *nekim* is rare. The NET Bible lists options: "stricken ones," "foreigners," or emending to "attackers" (from a root meaning "to strike"). The ancient versions all read an active sense (LXX: "whips"; Symmachus: "smiters"). The passive "abjects" (KJV) comes from the medieval Rabbi Kimchi. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

Spurgeon vividly pictures the scene: "Like curs around a sick lion, the mean wretches taunted and insulted one whose name had been their terror … A pack of dogs tearing their prey is nothing compared with a set of malicious gossips mauling the reputation of a worthy man." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 16 — "Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me."**

Another difficult verse. Ellicott explains two main approaches: (1) the older rendering: "profane jesters of cakes" — i.e., ribald parasites at a rich man's table who mock for a meal (the Pulpit Commentary takes this view); (2) the rendering many modern scholars prefer: "with profanity and barbarism" (treating the word as related to "stammering" or foreign speech in Isaiah 28:11), pointing to the anti-national party that adopted foreign ways. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-35.html)

Spurgeon sees Christ's passion in this: "Very forcibly might our Lord have used the words of these verses! Let us not forget to see the Despised and Rejected of men here painted to the life. Calvary and the ribald crew around the cross seem brought before our eyes." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 17 — "How long, O Lord, will You look on? Rescue my soul from their ravages, my precious life from these lions."**

The "How long?" cry is common in the psalms. The Pulpit Commentary notes that "man desires immediate deliverance; God mostly delays his deliverance until Patience has 'had her perfect work' (James 1:4)." The "lions" image recalls Psalm 22:20–21. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-35.html)

The BSB "my precious life" translates Hebrew *yechidati* ("my only one," "my darling"). The NET Bible notes the psalmist may mean his life is precious or that he feels isolated and alone. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28)

Spurgeon: "We may thus reason with the Lord. He permits us this familiarity." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 18 — "Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people."**

This closes the second section of the psalm. Spurgeon: "Notable deliverances must be recorded, and their fame emblazoned … Most men publish their griefs, good men should proclaim their mercies." Guzik notes David vowed public thanksgiving, not private. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

---

**v. 19 — "Let not my enemies gloat over me without cause, nor those who hate me without reason wink in malice."**

Jesus applies this verse to Himself in John 15:25: "They hated me without a cause." Guzik, citing VanGemeren: "Jesus identified with those who suffer without apparent cause." Gill likewise sees this as a direct messianic connection. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

"Wink with the eye" (or "wink in malice") was a gesture of deceitful conspiracy. Poole (via Guzik): "Wink with their eye, i.e. mock me, or insult over me, as the phrase signifies, Proverbs 6:13; 10:10." Ellicott calls it "a common gesture of agreement among confederates." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

---

**v. 20 — "For they do not speak peace, but they devise deceitful schemes against those who live quietly in the land."**

"The quiet ones in the land" (*die Stillen im Lande* in Luther's German Bible) became a key phrase in German Pietism, describing believers who withdraw from worldly ambition and trust God to defend them. Guzik quotes F.B. Meyer: "In every age God has had his quiet ones. Retired from its noise and strife, withdrawn from its ambitions and jealousies, unshaken by its alarms; because they had entered into the secret of a life hidden in God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Spurgeon: "David would fain have been an orderly citizen, but they laboured to make him a rebel … This is an old trick of the enemy to brand good men … as sowers of sedition, though they have ever been a harmless race, like sheep among wolves." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 21 — "They gape at me and say, 'Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!'"**

Spurgeon: "Malice has but one eye; it is blind to all virtue in its enemy. Eyes can generally see what hearts wish. A man with a mote in his eye sees a spot in the sun." He calls their "Aha!" the laugh of a hyena over a good man's slips. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

The NET Bible notes that "our eye sees" is apparently an idiom meaning "to look in triumph" or "gloat over." (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+35%3A1-28)

---

**v. 22 — "O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me."**

Guzik notes that two different Hebrew names for God are used here: *Yahweh* (LORD in small capitals, the covenant name) and *Adonai* (Lord in regular letters, meaning Master/Sir). David appeals to both God's covenant faithfulness and His sovereign authority. Kidner: "'Thou hast seen' is a perfect foil to the enemy's cry, 'our eyes have seen it!'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Spurgeon: "Our heavenly Father knows all our sorrow. Omniscience is the saint's candle which never goes out. A father will not long endure to see his child abused." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 23 — "Awake and rise to my defense, to my cause, my God and my Lord!"**

The call for God to "awake" is not literal (as though God were asleep) but an impassioned appeal. The Pulpit Commentary: "The psalmists call on God to awake … as a sort of stirring appeal to him to arise and manifest himself." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-35.html)

Guzik notes David uses *Elohim* here ("my God") alongside *Adonai* ("my Lord"). Spurgeon observes that "My God and my Lord" is the same cry Thomas uttered seeing the wounds of Jesus (John 20:28): "If he did not count our Lord to be divine, neither does David here ascribe Deity to Jehovah, for there is no difference except in the order of the words and the tongue in which they were spoken; the meaning is identical." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 24 — "Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God, and do not let them gloat over me."**

David does not ask for vindication on the basis of his own righteousness but on God's. The Pulpit Commentary: "Let thy law of righteousness be the rule by which I am judged, and my enemies also." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-35.html)

---

**v. 25 — "Let them not say in their hearts, 'Aha, just what we wanted!' Let them not say, 'We have swallowed him up!'"**

The enemies' imagined triumph is preempted by prayer. Spurgeon: "Saints are too dear a morsel for the powers of evil; God will not give his sheep over to the wolfish jaws of the persecutors … They reckon without their host … Their bird shall be flown, and they themselves shall be in the trap." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 26 — "May those who gloat in my distress be ashamed and confounded; may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach."**

Spurgeon: "God will make little of them, though they 'magnified themselves;' he will shame them for shaming his people, bring them to confusion for making confusion, pull off their fine apparel and give them a beggarly suit of dishonour, and turn all their rejoicing into weeping and wailing, and gnashing of teeth. Truly, the saints can afford to wait." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 27 — "May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness; may they always say, 'Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant's well-being.'"**

David's vindication is ultimately for the glory of God and the joy of the believing community. Guzik, citing Poole: "Mine enemies' great design is to magnify themselves, verse 26, but my chief desire is that God may be magnified." Maclaren (via Guzik) stresses: "His own deliverance, not the other's destruction, makes the singer joyful in Jehovah." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

Spurgeon: "We can have no nobler title than 'servant of God,' and no greater reward than for our Master to delight in our prosperity." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

---

**v. 28 — "Then my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness and Your praises all day long."**

The psalm ends not on enemies or self but on unceasing praise of God. Spurgeon: "From morning till evening the grateful tongue would talk and sing, and glorify the Lord." Guzik: "David spoke much of his own need and trouble in this psalm. Yet he ended with a strong focus on God and His praise." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

---

## Tradition-Specific Differences and Other Views

### Authorship / Date

**Traditional (Davidic):** Gill, Spurgeon, Guzik, and the Pulpit Commentary all hold to Davidic authorship during the Sauline persecution, citing the match between v. 1 and 1 Samuel 24:15, and the life-of-David details in vv. 11–17.

**Modern critical (non-Davidic):** Ellicott represents the view that "few good critics consider the psalm Davidic." He suggests it may be from Jeremiah's time, or from the post-exilic community facing Persian/Grecian influence, based on the "anti-national party" language in v. 16 and the communal rather than individual feel of the psalm. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

### The Angel of the LORD (vv. 5–6)

- **Preincarnate Christ view (Evangelical/Pentecostal):** Guzik, citing Boice, states this is "a preincarnate manifestation of the second person of the Trinity, the Lord Jesus Christ." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

- **Personified natural force (critical):** Ellicott says "there can be little doubt that the 'angel of Jehovah' … is a personification of the 'hurricane' itself." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

- **Good or evil angel (older Reformed):** Gill allows for either a good angel or "an evil angel … employed by the Lord, as the executioner of his wrath." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)

### The Imprecatory Problem

- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** Robust defence — these are not personal vendettas but prayers for divine justice. "Squeamish sentimentality may object to the strong language here used, but in their hearts all good men wish confusion to mischief-makers." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** More nuanced — acknowledges a tension between Old Testament and Christian ethics: "that longing for retributive justice which in an individual becomes, in a Christian view, wickedly vindictive, but to the Old Testament Church was the vindication of the Divine honour which was pledged to do justice to the chosen but afflicted people." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

- **Pentecostal/Evangelical (Guzik):** Treats the imprecations as prayers applicable to spiritual enemies (the devil and demons) for the believer today, citing 1 Timothy 3:7, 2 Timothy 2:26, and 2 Corinthians 2:11 as grounds for praying that Satan be caught in his own snares. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)

### "My prayer returned into mine own bosom" (v. 13)

- **Spurgeon:** Prayer is never wasted — it blesses the one who prays even if it does not benefit the one prayed for. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps035.php)
- **Gill:** Either David prayed privately and was heard, or his prayer was rejected/despised by his enemies and returned to him. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/35.htm)
- **Ellicott (and Delitzsch/Ewald):** The prayer was repeated again and again, or literally muttered into his bowed bosom. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/35.htm)

### "The quiet ones in the land" (v. 20)

Luther's German Bible translated this as *die Stillen im Lande*, which became a significant phrase in German Pietism to describe believers who cultivate a hidden life of devotion, withdrawn from worldly ambition. Guzik cites F.B. Meyer's devotional expansion of this theme. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-35/)
